name: Fuel lantern (white-gas, propane, kerosene and wick)

fuels: other fuels only as the lantern's own label names them (unleaded petrol on Dual Fuel models, propane, kerosene, lamp oil)
combustion.note: Coleman says its pressure lanterns are for outdoor use only: they use up oxygen and are not heaters. For wick lanterns check the maker's label: Health Canada says not to use oil lamps in enclosed areas unless designed for indoor use.

comps.spec: Glass globe round the mantle, under the ventilator; Coleman says to wrap it separately when a lantern is sent for service
comps.loc: Between the ventilator and the base

comps.spec: Fuel tank (fount) with filler cap: holds the fuel under pump pressure on pressure lanterns; on wick lanterns an unpressurised oil tank in the base
White gas, kerosene or lamp oil left in the tank, and spare cans nearby. White-gas-only Coleman lanterns: never kerosene or car fuel
Generator tube from the fuel valve up to the burner on pressure lanterns; part of the brightness control is inside it, so it is replaced when the lantern won't turn down
comps.loc: Inside the globe, under the burner

comps.spec: Hand air pump in the tank: plunger, pump cup, check valve and air stem. About 30 strokes; oil the cup now and then
Fuel valve with a knob that sets brightness; propane lanterns have a regulator valve instead
comps.loc: Top of the tank, under the globe

comps.spec: Ventilator hood with bail handle, and a heat shield; the top of the lantern gets hot
comps.loc: Top of the lantern, held by a ball nut

comps.spec: Disposable propane cylinder on propane lanterns, often part full. Never refill a disposable cylinder

notes: Coleman's white-gas lanterns are for outdoor use only: they burn up oxygen, make carbon monoxide, and are not space heaters. Spare mantles in old boxes, and some imported ones, may contain radioactive thorium; the risk is from breathing in or swallowing the ash, so wash your hands after changing one (JSP 392). A burned mantle is very fragile and breaks if touched, and a mantle with a hole lets the lantern overheat.
